passages.title: Self-Driving Cars: Ready for Our Roads?
text: Self-driving cars, which use cameras, sensors, and artificial intelligence to drive without human control, are already being tested in several countries. Some cities in the United States and China even allow driverless taxis to carry passengers. As the technology develops, many people are asking whether such vehicles should be allowed on public roads everywhere.

Supporters argue that self-driving cars could save many lives. According to studies of road accidents, the great majority of crashes are caused at least partly by human error, such as speeding, tiredness, or using a phone while driving. A computer never gets sleepy or distracted, and it can react faster than a human. In addition, self-driving cars could give independence to people who cannot drive, such as older people and people with disabilities.

Opponents, however, believe the technology is not yet ready. Self-driving systems still struggle in heavy rain, on roads without clear markings, and in unpredictable situations, such as a child suddenly running into the street or a police officer directing traffic by hand. Several serious accidents involving test vehicles have raised questions about who is responsible when a driverless car causes harm: the owner, the manufacturer, or the software company?

There are also concerns about jobs and security. Millions of people earn a living as drivers of taxis, buses, and trucks, and widespread automation could leave many of them unemployed. Moreover, cars controlled by software could, in theory, be hacked.

In conclusion, self-driving cars offer real benefits, but important safety, legal, and social questions remain unanswered. A gradual approach, starting with limited areas and clear laws on responsibility, may be the most sensible way forward.

passages.title: Should Online Games Be Limited for Teenagers?
text: Online games are among the most popular forms of entertainment for teenagers. Some countries, such as China, have introduced strict rules limiting how many hours young people may play each week. This has sparked a debate in many other countries about whether similar limits are needed.

Those in favour of limits are mainly concerned about health and education. Spending long hours in front of a screen is linked to poor sleep, lack of physical activity, and eye strain. Some teenagers play late into the night and struggle to concentrate at school the next day. In a small number of cases, gaming becomes a serious problem; the World Health Organization recognizes "gaming disorder" as a condition in which a person loses control over gaming despite negative consequences.

Those against limits argue that most young people play games in a healthy way. For them, games are a way to relax, to spend time with friends, and even to develop skills such as problem-solving, teamwork, and English. They also point out that the gaming industry offers career opportunities, from game design to professional e-sports. Above all, they believe that decisions about free time should be made by families, not by governments.

Some experts suggest a middle path. Instead of strict national limits, they recommend that parents and teenagers agree on reasonable rules together, such as no gaming after a certain time on school nights. Game companies could also help by including features that remind players to take breaks.
Ultimately, the question is not whether games are good or bad, but how to make sure they remain a healthy part of teenagers' lives.

passages.title: Nuclear Power for Indonesia?
text: Indonesia plans to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2060, and the government has included nuclear power in its long-term energy plans. The idea is not new; it has been discussed for decades. Yet it remains one of the most controversial energy questions in the country.

Advocates of nuclear power emphasize its reliability. Unlike solar and wind power, a nuclear plant can produce large amounts of electricity day and night, regardless of the weather. It also produces almost no greenhouse gases while operating. For a country trying to reduce its dependence on coal while meeting rising demand, this steady, low-carbon supply is attractive. Supporters also note that Indonesia has trained nuclear scientists and has safely operated research reactors for many years.

Opponents, however, raise serious concerns. The most obvious is safety. Indonesia lies on the Pacific Ring of Fire and frequently experiences earthquakes and tsunamis. The 2011 disaster at the Fukushima plant in Japan, which was caused by a tsunami, showed how dangerous such events can be for nuclear facilities. Critics also point to the problem of radioactive waste, which remains dangerous for thousands of years and requires secure long-term storage.

Cost is another issue. Nuclear plants are extremely expensive to build and often take more than ten years to complete, with frequent delays and budget increases. Some argue that the same money could deliver more electricity, more quickly, if it were invested in solar, geothermal, and hydropower.

Both sides agree that Indonesia needs more clean energy. The disagreement lies in whether nuclear power's benefits outweigh its risks and costs. Any decision will require careful site selection, strict regulation, and, above all, the trust of the public.

questions.question: What kind of text is Self-Driving Cars: Ready for Our Roads?

options.A: A narrative about a driverless taxi
options.B: A recount of a car accident
options.C: A procedure explaining how to drive
options.D: A discussion presenting views for and against an issue

questions.explanation: Teks memuat isu (paragraf 1), argumen pendukung (paragraf 2), argumen penentang (paragraf 3–4), dan simpulan. Inilah struktur discussion text.

questions.question: According to supporters, why could self-driving cars save lives?

options.A: They are cheaper than ordinary cars.
options.B: They are controlled by police officers.
options.C: They can only be used in limited areas.
options.D: Most crashes involve human error, which computers avoid.

questions.explanation: Paragraf 2: sebagian besar kecelakaan melibatkan kesalahan manusia, sedangkan komputer tidak mengantuk atau terdistraksi.

Decide whether each point is a benefit or a concern raised in the text.
(1) Independence for people who cannot drive

(3) Possible job losses among drivers

options.B: Parking in a well-marked car park
options.C: Keeping a steady speed on an empty road

options.C: Replacing all taxis with driverless vehicles immediately

questions.question:
